item.title: Pet Grief in Older Adults: Finding Comfort Through Faith
item.description:
The loss of a pet is devastating at any age, but for older adults, the grief can carry a weight that is hard to understand. After decades of life experiences, most people seem to think that older adults have developed the ability to face grief more easily than the rest of us. The reality is more complex.

When an older adult loses a pet that has been part of their daily lives for many years, they can feel overwhelmed by the grief. If a pet has been their constant companion through retirement, illness, or the loss of a spouse, this loss can be painful and lonely. The good news is that this pain can be an opportunity to lean into the grace of God and know how His comfort will extend to their heart.

The Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, NIV

Understanding the Depth of Pet Grief in Older Adults

Culture tells us that some losses aren’t that important. For older adults, this message creates a hard situation when they are devastated by the loss of a pet and question the legitimacy of their pain. Pet loss is often dismissed as something that should be sad but easy to get over. This reflects a deeper assumption about aging and emotional resilience that keeps older adults disconnected from their unique emotional experiences.

Many older adults have connections with their pets that go beyond companionship. Their pets have become part of their daily routine and the reason they get up each morning. Some adults have no one else in their lives, so their furry friends have become the only one who depends on them.

When there are no adult children nearby, and a spouse has passed away, a pet will fill the void and go beyond friendship. These loving pets will create a purpose and show unconditional love. This will create a sense of being needed for the older adult who is now the caregiver for this living creature.

The grief of pet loss can often mimic that of human relationships. The shock of the silence when there is no barking or purring that once resonated creates a lonely silence for the owner. There may be feelings of guilt due to decisions regarding life-ending care. Anger is common as the world continues to be okay, while the pet owner feels devastated. The contradiction of these feelings creates a sense of falling apart, even though they look fine to those around them.

Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. – Matthew 5:4, NIV

When Grief Feels Overwhelming and Isolating

Pet grief in older adults is often accompanied by isolation. This isolation is a response to well-meaning suggestions that seem hurtful to those who have lost their companion. Some family and friends may suggest getting another pet, but this doesn’t negate the pain they feel about the unique pet they just lost.

These suggestions can create a sense of emotional isolation because others don’t understand how special their pet was. While people often mean well, this message conveys that the pain isn’t worthy of respect. The dismissive attitude of this mindset creates a hidden burden for older adults who are already struggling with multiple losses and health challenges.

The pet that was by their side daily and provided emotional support during difficult times is no longer present, and the grief is being compounded by the feeling that the grief should be hidden. Some older adults feel embarrassed about the depth of their grief and end up isolating themselves and navigating the grieving process in silence.

The practical aspect adds another layer of complexity. The bills for veterinary care, cremation costs, and the physical demands of caring for an ill pet bring with them a level of stress that goes beyond the emotional pain. Adults with fixed incomes or limited mobility often feel like these challenges are impossible to overcome, creating a tangled web of feelings of helplessness, regret, and grief.

Christian counselors understand that this type of complicated grief requires a gentle process. They recognize that the shame associated with pet loss is often the reason older adults dismiss the thought of getting support. As a result, a generation of older adults feels they must process loss and dismiss validation.

Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:4, NIV

Finding Comfort in Faith During Pet Loss

Faith can offer a unique perspective on pet loss and be a profound comfort during the grieving process. The God who created every creature with purpose and love understands the bonds that older adults form with their companions.

Scripture doesn’t minimize these relationships but rather points to a Creator who values all of His creation. This understanding can encourage older adults to find peace in knowing their grief is acknowledged by a Father who understands.

Prayer can be a powerful tool for processing the complex emotions of pet loss. Unlike human relationships that can come with complications and unfinished business, relationships with pets often represent pure love and acceptance. When this kind of pain is brought to God in prayer, the outcome is an honest expression of loss without the need to justify your feelings to those who may not understand.

It often helps older adults view their role as pet caregivers through a spiritual lens. When a person takes on the responsibility of caring for another living being of God’s creation and shows compassion during illness, it reflects Christian love in action. This is a transformative perspective that can turn feelings of guilt or regret into a recognition of faithful stewardship.

Christian counselors often assist with this situation by encouraging the exploration of faith and its relationship with loss and grief. This process involves acknowledging that love creates vulnerability to pain, but that pain is not meaningless in suffering. In times of loss, the pain becomes an opportunity to experience God’s comfort in new depths. This helps us understand how He connects with us during our grieving process.

Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those who are in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God. – 2 Corinthians 1:3-4, NIV

Moving Forward with Hope and Healing

Healing from pet loss doesn’t mean forgetting or minimizing the relationship that was lost. Rather, it involves learning to carry the love and memories forward while allowing space for life to continue. The process often requires patience and recognizing that grief has no predetermined timeline or proper way to unfold.

Some practical steps can help older adults process the grief of losing their furry loved one. By doing these things, grief can be transformed into a special remembrance that can help provide closure for the loss of the relationship. A few ideas are:

  • Plant a garden
  • Create a photo album
  • Donate to an animal shelter
  • Create a memorial space for the pet

Faith communities can also support older adults through pet grief. If a church acknowledges that these losses are just as important as other losses that people experience, then that church community is validating the pain and creating a network of support. There have been some instances of churches finding meaningful ways to honor the role of pets through blessing ceremonies or memorial services.

Christian counselors emphasize that moving forward after pet loss doesn’t mean immediate action or decisions about future pets. The focus is on processing the current loss and allowing God’s comfort to work through the natural grieving process. Some older adults may find peace in opening their hearts to another pet companion, while others feel they need to follow a different healing path.

The journey through pet loss grief can ultimately deepen faith and the understanding of God’s compassion. Many times, these older adults feel closer to God after walking through a hard season of loss through tangibly experiencing His comfort.

“For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the LORD, “plans to prosper you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future.” – Jeremiah 29:11, NIV

Consider Support

Pet grief in older adults reflects a depth of love and connection, demonstrating the capacity for relationship and care. Faith offers comfort and a fresh perspective, allowing older adults to honor their grief and love, finding solace in God’s promise of comfort.

Christian counselors can help them navigate pain through understanding what God says about grief. This allows for a more natural healing process rather than one that is hidden because the loss is culturally less important.

For help with pet loss grief in your area, contact your local Christian counseling services to set up an appointment.

item.title: Teen Anxiety, Virtual Reality, and the Inner World of Teen Boys
item.description:
Teen boys often struggle with anxiety even before they develop a life consumed with social media and virtual reality technology. It begins when they are subjected to the pressure to perform, fit in, and stay strong.

Virtual reality (sometimes called VR), gaming, social spaces, and other immersive worlds are beginning to blur the line between escape and harmful avoidance. Virtual reality can ease or intensify teen anxiety, and parents don’t always know what to look for.

How Virtual Reality Impacts Teen Anxiety

Most teen boys choose to escape through virtual reality because it feels like a safe place where they are in control of their environment. They can win the battles and avoid real-life interactions. Many teens feel as though virtual reality is a relief from the anxiety they struggle with daily.

Within the worlds of this technology, they find structure, clear rules, and feedback that they don’t get in real life. These experiences can lower stress and give their minds a break from the constant worries of grades, friendships, and their future.

The appeal to virtual reality is deeper than just a simple distraction. Virtual reality offers teen boys something that feels like certainty in a world that is constantly shifting beneath their feet. The digital world responds with consistency, even though anxiety makes social situations unpredictable and overwhelming.

In virtual reality, the focus becomes levels to complete, achievements to unlock, and avatars that represent who they wish they could be. This is a sense of mastery that can feel like relief when everyday life leaves them feeling powerless and unseen.

There is a new complexity to the connection between virtual reality and anxiety. Some professionals in clinical settings are now using virtual reality-based therapies to reduce anxiety, teach coping skills, and practice facing fearful situations in a controlled way. However, there is concern that being immersed in heavy digital platforms, such as virtual reality, can intensify depression, addiction-like patterns, and social withdrawal in vulnerable adolescents.

Virtual reality doesn’t create teen anxiety, but it can shape how it is expressed. Teens who spend more time in virtual spaces than in real relationships carry their fears and insecurities with them into virtual reality. Once the headset is on, they have fewer chances to practice in-person problem-solving and emotional regulation. The result is a deepened avoidance that makes ordinary situations feel more overwhelming.

When Virtual Reality Offers Help for Teen Anxiety

The other side of this situation is that mental health professionals are exploring ways to use virtual reality as a tool. There are programs in which teens enter carefully designed virtual environments to practice skills for handling anxiety, managing their thoughts, and calming their bodies. By facing specific fears in a gradual, supported way, the goal is to use virtual reality as a bridge between avoidance and real-life engagement.

While the teen is engaged in this type of treatment, they can:

  • Notice how anxiety feels in their body.
  • Learn and practice breathing and grounding skills while they remain in a stressful scene.
  • Understand that strong emotions rise and fall instead of remaining at a constant peak.

Some teen boys find that the structured practice reduces the sense that anxiety is stronger than they are. They begin to discover they can stay present, make eye contact, and complete complex tasks, even though they are in the middle of anxiety. Under thoughtful and careful guidance, virtual reality can support existing therapies rather than replace them.

Christian counselors incorporate this kind of technology alongside talk therapy, prayer, and Scripture to help anxious teens move toward healing. Reminders like this one in Psalm 4 can help teen boys learn to trust God:

In peace I will both lie down and sleep, For You alone, Lord, have me dwell in safety. – Psalm 4:8, NASB

When Virtual Reality Deepens Isolation in Teen Anxiety

Virtual reality is not therapeutic in every instance. Some teen boys use headsets primarily for gaming or for social platforms that lack built-in safeguards. After long hours online, sleep is crowded out, and exercise, homework, and family time come to a halt. Teens who are already struggling with anxiety become trapped in a pattern that quietly reinforces their fears and keeps them from overcoming anxiety.

These teen boys begin to feel that the only way to be valued is to rely on virtual victories. They often avoid real-life situations that could lead to failure or embarrassment. Real-life school situations, such as stress and bullying, lead to the teen finding a safe place in the headset where the harsh and cruel reality is muted. The result is a growing distance between their everyday life and their online identity.

This shift doesn’t happen overnight. It is a gradual process in which the teen boy who once spent time with friends begins to decline the invitation to hang out. The conversations at dinner become short and sometimes defensive as these teens spend more hours in virtual reality.

What started as a way to unwind becomes a primary means of survival. The virtual world becomes a place where this adolescent feels more connected to himself as real-life relationships become more strained and distant.

When teens become immersed in the virtual reality world, parents may notice irritability when asked to turn off the system, declining grades, or trading sleep for late-night engagement in virtual reality. Another significant sign is that they have withdrawn from friendships. These can indicate that anxiety or sadness is driving the teen to use virtual reality for more than just straightforward enjoyment.

Christian counselors help families slow down and ask honest, gentle questions about why the teen boy feels the need to escape. The goal becomes understanding the pain beneath the use of virtual reality rather than shaming its use.

Walking with Anxious Teen Boys in a Virtual Reality World

Connecting with teen boys in a world of virtual reality requires more than just setting screen time limits. Parents are encouraged to listen patiently, develop wise boundaries, and be willing to enter their world without negating their struggles.

For teen boys who struggle with anxiety, the conversation about virtual reality use can be more effective when focused on their inner experience. Through thoughtful and gentle questions, parents can open a door to talk about shame, fear of failure, or loneliness that some teen boys may not know how to name.

Christian counselors assist families in developing practical plans that will include a healthy routine and carefully chosen virtual reality experiences to support growth rather than increase avoidance. Some treatment plans may include collaboration with mental health providers who specialize in virtual reality-based interventions. This will allow technology to be aligned with therapeutic goals in a faith-based treatment plan.

The process of healing includes developing a stronger sense of who they are beyond the screen. This requires them to identify what they value, what brings them genuine connection, and what helps them feel capable in the real world.

Christian counselors help families focus on rebuilding patterns of engagement to honor the teen, his struggles, and his need for an authentic relationship. The goal is to restore balance and help the team recognize that his anxiety does not define him.

Teen boys struggling with anxiety need to know that their worth is not measured by their performance in games, their social status at school, or their ability to hide how much they worry. Christian counselors help these boys recognize that their identity is grounded in Christ, who sees their hidden fears and invites them to bring their anxious thoughts into the light.

If you’d like to learn more about supporting your teen, connect with this office. A receptionist can tell you more about the counseling services offered.

item.title: The Complexities of Dating Someone with Bipolar Disorder
item.description:
There are two truths to dating someone with bipolar disorder. Firstly, it is an experience that not everyone will be open to, and secondly, it can be one of the deepest, most meaningful experiences of your life. The determining factor is how well equipped you are to handle the intense ups and downs that come with the territory of bipolar disorder.

Dating someone with bipolar disorder requires open communication, clear boundaries, and realistic expectations. You will only manage to do any of these things when you are familiar with the disorder in general and when you understand how and to what degree it affects your partner. Having a romantic partner with bipolar disorder requires you to love them in the specific way they need to be loved, and to guard yourself.

Ups and Downs in the Relationship

Most people have baggage, residual trauma, and insecurities that bring tension and conflict into a relationship. However, people with bipolar disorder have a mood-altering disorder that acts as a magnifying glass to all of their self-doubts and fears. It’s not uncommon for someone with bipolar disorder to either shy away from romantic connections entirely or else enter into them with a lot of trepidation.

It’s impossible to love someone who won’t allow themselves to be loved. Dating someone with bipolar disorder often means having to be more patient than you realized you could be. You should be prepared for the manic and depressive episodes, and the way your loved one seems to change with either one.

It will require a lot of grace. You must anticipate the hurtful things they will say when manic, and try not to take them personally. You must also prepare for the times when they become emotionally distant and shut you out because they are overwhelmed with shame and exhaustion during their depressive spells.

One of the first things you must consider as you begin dating someone with bipolar disorder is how they are handling the disorder. Some people have been diagnosed for years, are receiving treatment, have a good idea about their triggers, and can roughly anticipate the rhythms of the disorder.

If this is the case, you will be much better prepared for the ups and downs because your partner is prepared for them. Communication will be more open, and there will be less shame and embarrassment involved.

However, some people have either not been diagnosed or are not coping well with their diagnosis. They have little regard for treatment and don’t even attempt to help themselves or their loved ones during mania or depression.

It is harder to be romantically involved with people who take this approach to bipolar disorder because you cannot set boundaries as easily, or support them without draining your personal resources. No relationship can survive when one party has a disregard for their own health and their loved one’s happiness, regardless of whatever disorders are at play.

Practical Things You Can Do at the Start of the Relationship

One of the first steps you must take when dating someone with bipolar disorder is to familiarize yourself with the condition. Do as much research on the topic as you can. Ask your partner questions about their experience, but only do so when they are in a stable mood. Show that you are curious, non-judging, and open to learning so that you can better support them.

More important than doing research or even asking questions is listening. Take note each time they open up about their experience, knowing that no website can teach you as accurately as your partner can when it comes to their lived experience. Listen to what they share concerning what their episodes feel like, and what helps and what doesn’t help.

When it’s appropriate and when they are in a stable mood, have a conversation about their triggers and patterns. Try to determine any early warning signs for a manic episode, such as periods of stress or anger. You will have to figure out how best to respond to these triggers, knowing that there’s not necessarily a way to help them avoid an episode. Knowing their triggers is more of a benefit to you, so that you can anticipate what happens next.

When dating someone with bipolar disorder, one of your major roles will be that of caretaker. It is not a constant role. The disorder is not static and changes somewhat regularly. Bipolar disorder is treatable with medication, which brings emotional balance, and therapy, which helps with their long-term outlook. You can help by encouraging treatment, following up about medication, and accompanying them to doctors’ appointments, if they invite you.

Lastly, in the beginning stages of dating someone with bipolar disorder, it is essential to remember to keep your own life intact. Every healthy relationship is made up of two individuals with unique interests, hobbies, responsibilities, and a life outside of the relationship. It’s easy to let the high demands of a relationship like this become consuming. You must maintain a life outside of the relationship, and do so from the start.

Strapping In for the Long Haul

You cannot maintain a successful long-term relationship unless you take care of yourself. Regardless of how well they manage the disorder, being in a relationship with someone with bipolar disorder often means dealing with volatility, caregiver fatigue, and emotional exhaustion. There are several important boundaries you must establish as soon as you see the relationship deepening.

Firstly, it’s important to learn to use ‘I’ statements when establishing boundaries, but also when simply expressing yourself in the relationship. Talk about your experience, your limitations, and your concerns by prefacing statements with “I.” “I feel like I’m the only one making an effort here,” or “I will not tolerate threats, regardless of what episode you are going through,” for example. Establishing boundaries is about protecting yourself, not about changing, shaming, or controlling your partner.

Secondly, never attempt to have important conversations like these during either depressive or manic episodes. Your partner needs to be in a clear frame of mind so that they can fully understand what is being established, with no clouded judgment. You need to be selective about when you have certain discussions when you are dating someone with bipolar disorder.

You must decide and communicate what behavior you will not accept, regardless of whatever episode they are going through. During a manic episode, your partner might say cutting things, accuse you of things you have never done, or become threatening and physically intimidating. They will likely regret everything once the episode passes, but you are never obligated to receive this kind of treatment.

Have an honest conversation about what you will do in the event of them saying hurtful things during mania. Consider having zero tolerance for abusive language, physical aggression, threats, reckless spending, or cheating, all of which commonly happen during manic episodes.

One of the most common areas to affect any relationship, especially in the long term, is finances. People in a manic episode tend to become overly generous and impulsive, and this can cause many financial issues. It’s a good idea to have separate bank accounts for this reason and to refuse their access to your personal funds.

You might also have to consider whether you will help them manage any debts incurred during a manic episode, keeping in mind that you are not obligated to if you have separate accounts.

Lastly, pay attention to your own needs and be generous with yourself. Ensure that you are getting quality sleep, plenty of time with friends, a healthy diet, and enough time alone. While you might not have the same mental health struggles as your partner, your well-being is every bit as important as theirs.

If you are dating someone with bipolar disorder, you could greatly benefit from counseling. You don’t have to go through things alone. We hope that you will be able to find a counselor either by consulting our online catalog or by speaking with someone on our reception team.

item.title: When Your Mind Jumps to the Worst-Case Scenario: Understanding Catastrophizing
item.description:
Have you ever found yourself jumping to the worst-case scenario before you have all the facts? Your phone rings unexpectedly late at night. Your supervisor asks if you have “a few minutes to talk.” Your child doesn’t reply to your text as quickly as usual. Your spouse answers your question briefly before walking away. Before you’ve had a chance to gather the facts, your mind has already written the story’s ending.

Something is wrong. I’m in trouble. They’re upset with me. Maybe I really can’t do anything right. If this sounds familiar, you may be experiencing catastrophizing.

Catastrophizing is more than simply “overthinking.” It is a pattern of assuming the worst possible outcome before there is enough evidence to support that conclusion. These thoughts often feel convincing, urgent, and overwhelming, making it difficult to slow down or consider other possibilities.

How does research define catastrophizing?

Cognitive therapist Aaron Beck, one of the pioneers of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), describes catastrophizing as “dwelling on the worst possible outcomes of any situation in which there is a possibility for an unpleasant outcome. The person overemphasizes the probability of this catastrophic outcome and usually exaggerates the possible consequences of its occurrence” (Beck et al., 1985).

Put simply, catastrophizing is a thinking pattern that can show up when we feel vulnerable, uncertain, unsafe, or out of control. It can contribute to panic attacks, racing thoughts, shortness of breath, feelings of helplessness, trouble thinking clearly, and even increased pain severity (Turner & Aaron, 2001).

For some people, the spiral happens so quickly that they hardly notice it. One uncomfortable emotion or unanswered question can instantly cause the mind to prepare for a disaster. At times, catastrophic thoughts can create a sense of urgency or leave you feeling frozen, unable to think clearly or decide what to do next.

A feeling of discomfort or uncertainty can lead the mind to prepare for the worst possible outcome, even when there is little evidence to support that the outcome is likely to happen.

Three Parts of Catastrophizing

Research by Cox (2021) describes catastrophizing as involving three common experiences: helplessness, rumination, and magnification. Understanding these patterns can help you recognize whether they show up in your own thought process.

Helplessness 

Helplessness is the belief that nothing can be done to improve a situation or change the outcome.

It may sound like:

There’s no way to fix this.

Nothing I do will make a difference.

When we feel helpless, it’s easy to overlook the ways we’ve handled difficult situations before. We may forget the support, skills, and resources that are still available to us or assume that no solution applies to our situation.

Psychologist Martin Seligman’s work on learned helplessness explains why people sometimes stop believing their actions can make a difference, even when opportunities for change are present (Seligman, 1972). Over time, the more we believe we lack control, the harder it becomes to recognize the choices and strengths we still have.

Rumination

Rumination is the process of repeatedly thinking about the same uncomfortable thought, question, or situation without coming to a resolution. It can feel intrusive and overwhelming.

For some, rumination can look like replaying the same conversation over and over again because something feels unclear. Every detail gets analyzed. You wonder what you should have said differently. “Why did I say that?” Instead of gaining clarity, rumination can keep us stuck and feeling unable to move forward or consider other possibilities.

Magnification

Magnification often begins with a real concern that stretches into a catastrophe before there is evidence to support it. This is when the mind exaggerates the potential consequences or seriousness of a situation. A mistake at work can quickly turn into preparation for getting fired, rather than an error that can be corrected.

What Catastrophizing Can Sound Like

Catastrophizing can sound like:

What if he hates me?

What if she leaves me?

What if I embarrassed myself?

What if I fail and can’t recover?

What if I can’t do hard things?

What if they misunderstood what I meant?

These thoughts often reflect helplessness, rumination, and magnification working together. If you find yourself relating to this, you may be able to recognize that these thoughts often feel so believable that they become difficult to question. Your mind and body may begin preparing for or protecting you from danger before there is evidence that danger actually exists.

Why Our Mind Does This

There is not a single reason people catastrophize. For some, it may serve as a survival mechanism, preparing them for emotional hurt, rejection, or disappointment. If you can expect the worst, maybe it won’t hurt as much if it happens.

For individuals with a history of trauma, catastrophizing becomes the mind and body’s effort to stay safe. When someone experiences loss, pain, or danger, the nervous system learns to remain alert as it detects the next possible threat. While this response may have served as a protective response in the past, it may linger after the danger has passed.

Certain mental health conditions can also make catastrophic thinking more common. For example, the excessive worry that is typically associated with Generalized Anxiety Disorder can fuel “what if” thinking patterns.

Depression can make catastrophic predictions seem unavoidable because hopelessness or low self-esteem may shape the way a person sees the future.

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder frequently involves an intense need for certainty or reassurance, making catastrophic thinking difficult to control or ignore.

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder can keep the nervous system on high alert as a protective response, creating the belief that expecting the worst will somehow keep us safer.

It’s worth noting that people who struggle with catastrophizing do not automatically have these diagnoses. It simply means that catastrophizing can show up in different contexts for different people. Understanding the “why” behind these thought patterns can be a helpful first step to moving forward.

So, how do we stop this?

Let’s start here: the goal is not to eliminate every catastrophic thought. Instead, the goal is to recognize those thoughts, understand why they’re showing up, and learn to respond to them in ways that align with our values rather than allowing them to control us.

Here are a couple of CBT-based self-guided tools that may help.

Name the thought

Sometimes the first step is simply recognizing what is happening. This can look like telling yourself, “I am having a catastrophizing thought.” This small shift creates a distance between you and the thought. This gives you space to reconsider the situation and choose how you want to respond.

Ask, “What do I know for sure?”

Pause and reflect on the facts you know. Ask yourself: What do I know for certain? What am I assuming? What evidence supports this fear? What evidence suggests another possibility?

These questions are not to dismiss your fear, but to add a bit more clarity to your thought process.

Where Faith Comes In

For Christians, catastrophizing can create feelings of guilt and doubt about one’s faith. Some may ask, “If I trusted God more, would I still struggle with anxiety?” or “Does this mean my faith is weak?”

Throughout Scripture, we see faithful people experience fear, doubt, helplessness, and confusion. Yet throughout those moments, the Lord heard their cries and remained present. The same faithful God is with you in your anxiety. He sees your desire for safety and certainty.

His Word is a reminder of His steadiness and presence in the storm. We serve an intentional God who cares for even the smallest of His creation. If He feeds birds and clothes the lilies, then we can trust that He sees and responds to our needs too. Scripture tells us to come to Him, and He will give us rest (Matthew 11:28-30).

I’ll leave you with one final question: Is it possible for a thought to feel consuming, scary, and still not be factual?

If you find yourself overwhelmed by anxious, racing, or catastrophic thoughts, I would be glad to walk alongside you in this journey as you learn to understand what your fear may be trying to protect you from and develop more helpful ways of responding.

Give me a call to schedule an appointment today.

item.title: Cast Your Cares on the Lord: Scriptures to Help You Deal with Anxiety
item.description:
The Bible speaks often about anxiety, recognizing how it can take away our joy, sense of peace, and enjoyment of life. This is not how things were meant to be. We are each affected by the uncertainty of this world and our lives in different ways.

For some people, anxiety may be a mild inconvenience that they can overcome with some focus and effort. For others, anxiety may be an unbearable weight and a dark cloud that hangs over them daily, and that makes everyday tasks nearly impossible. Whatever the case, you can lean on God’s word to help you address your anxiety.

You may need additional help handling your anxiety, but a great place to start is with the abundant reminders of the Lord’s care for you.

God cares for you

Recognizing that God cares for you can be a great support during trying times. It’s something that we can pray or remind ourselves of in the moments when anxiety threatens to overwhelm and overtake us. We can find many verses in the Bible about how much God cares for us.

One of the key places to go is 1 Peter 5: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, that he may lift you up in due time. Cast all your anxiety on him because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:6-7, NIV) Peter is writing this to people experiencing terrible persecution, and many anxieties were stirred in the wake of that suffering.

Another passage that reminds us of God’s abundant care is Luke 12. When we are feeling fearful and concerned for our future, we are reminded by Jesus: “‘Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten by God. Indeed, the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Don’t be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.’” (Luke 12:6-7, NIV)

If God knows how many hairs are on our heads, rest assured that He knows our circumstances in minute detail and is looking upon us with attentive care. God cares for all of creation, but we are reminded here that He pays special attention to us.

One of the more well-known Bible passages reminds us of God’s care for us. It tells us that even in the direst circumstances, God is with us, so we don’t have to be afraid:

The LORD is my shepherd, I lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures, he leads me beside quiet waters, he refreshes my soul. He guides me along the right paths for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. – Psalm 23:1-4, NIV

Replacing Anxiety with Hope, Prayer, and Love

When anxiety crowds our hearts and minds, it eclipses everything else we may know to be true. Anxiety is your body’s natural response to stress. It is a feeling of fear or apprehension about things to come, whether a meeting, social occasion, job interview, or a date. A person who has an anxiety disorder will frequently have intense, excessive, and persistent worry and fear about everyday situations such as these.

An anxiety disorder requires treatment from a mental health professional, particularly if it begins to affect one’s life. Often, a therapeutic intervention called Cognitive Behavioral Therapy will be used. This is a form of talk therapy that helps a person identify any patterns of thought or behavior that negatively affect them and that do not align with reality.

Having identified those patterns, the therapist will help the person replace those patterns of thought and behavior with positive ones that promote their well-being.

To overcome anxiety, it’s not enough to name and understand the negative patterns and unhelpful thoughts that exacerbate the situation. Those thoughts need to be replaced. Some of the helpful thoughts and patterns of behavior can be drawn from Scripture. Below are a few examples that can help a person who struggles with anxiety.

Anxiety often drives a person inward, and once the spiral of negative thoughts begins, it can keep going endlessly. Instead of peering inward, one can look upward and outward, toward God.

Philippians 4 encourages us, saying, “Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6-7, NIV)

Turning one’s thoughts toward God and replacing anxious thoughts with prayer and thanksgiving can help develop a pattern of taking a positive outlook that lessens the grip of anxiety and allows one to rest in the peace of God.

Another helpful passage is from Jesus in Matthew 11.

“‘Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.’” – Matthew 11:28-30, NIV

In our anxiety, we often turn to other things in our thoughts and maybe even in our actions. Replacing that by approaching Jesus with our concerns can help us unburden ourselves when laying the outcome of our circumstances at His feet. He delights to relieve us of our cares.

Anxiety has the effect of suffocating hope and making a situation seem desperate beyond relief. This isn’t true, but our brains, beating hearts, sweaty palms, rapid breath, and tense muscles all say it is. But there is hope, whatever the situation, if our hope is in God. Though your body and your mind might be telling you something is true, the hope that is found in God can transcend even the darkest circumstances.

Why, my soul, are you downcast?
 Why so disturbed within me?
Put your hope in God,
for I will yet praise him,
my Savior and my God. – Psalm 42:11, NIV

God saves. The future, whatever it holds, can be hopeful because of who God is and what he has done in the past. Sometimes, if you are experiencing a panic attack, focusing your mind on something else can help you calm down. You can recite this verse or remind yourself of God’s rescues and the ways He’s saved you in the past to help you calm down.

Coming back full circle, it’s important to remember that we are loved. Our anxiety can have a rational root, but it can also be irrational and disproportionate to the circumstances. Either way, we are reminded of how much God loves us and just how safe we are in His hands.

Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or hardship or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? … No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. – Romans 8:35, 37-39, NIV

Finding Hope as You Cast Your Cares on the Lord

Anxiety can be a huge struggle that overwhelms your life and makes everyday tasks seem insurmountable. Anxiety can detract from your enjoyment of life and ability to do the things you’d like to do. If you are struggling with anxiety or an anxiety disorder, seek the help and support you need from a mental health professional. With a proper diagnosis and a treatment plan tailored for your needs, you can reclaim the peace that God intends for you.

Start by reaching out to our reception team to connect with me or another counselor who can help.

item.title: The Importance of Healthy Boundaries: Thoughts From a Christian Counselor
item.description:
Healthy boundaries are a necessary part of our lives, our relationships, and our mental health. Boundaries are frequently one of the things that we struggle with, not only setting but maintaining. We cannot have healthy relationships if we do not have healthy boundaries. When our relationships are unhealthy or even toxic, our boundaries are usually non-existent.

Why have boundaries?

Healthy boundaries mean that we can protect ourselves, our health – both mental and physical – as well as what is precious to us. They are the foundation of healthy relationships and are often invisible to others, but without them, the relationship will start to crumble from within. Boundaries are also a key part of your own self-care and making sure your needs are being met and not taken for granted.

Boundaries are not just important in romantic and familial relationships; they are also important in friendships, among colleagues, in business, and every aspect of your interactions with others. They allow you to protect yourself from ideas, opinions, and preconceptions of others, as well as give you the ability to voice your wants and needs in a healthy way.

Part of being human is having opinions, ideas, beliefs, biases, experiences, priorities, etc. While we are all allowed to have our own, often they conflict with those of others with whom we share bonds. This can create barriers, divisions, unequal dynamics, and fracturing relationships.

Boundaries need to be set with others for a variety of reasons, particularly because not everyone has our best interests at heart. Some may even be invested in your demise or your continuing toxicity because misery loves company. If you change, the other person may have to as well or face losing you altogether.

Proverbs 4:23 (NIV) “Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it.” Our hearts are precious and a gift from God. Our heart or soul is central to who we are, and we need to be careful who we let into it. This scripture instructs us to protect ourselves from things of this world and people who do not hold it as the precious gift it is.

Often, we engage in relationships with people who we know are not good for us. This can be partly because we don’t believe we are worthy of a healthy relationship. It can also be that we feel we need to rescue or help the other person or save them from themselves.

The trouble with this is that you must be a strong person to not be pulled down into the same behavior or negative thinking. This scripture also indicates that wounds to our heart can affect the core of who we are and our ability to function in the way God has called us to.

The Importance of Boundaries

Without boundaries, there is rarely mutual participation in the relationship, and one partner may end up giving more than the other. This can lead to resentment on one side and dependence on the other. Without boundaries the relationship between the two can end up in enmeshment, resentment, imbalance, codependence, and one person always giving where the other is always taking.

This leads to exhaustion on the part of the giver and dependence on the part of the taker. Both sides of the relationship may not always be aware of the imbalance until it is too late, causing anger and resentment, as well as a potential breakdown of the relationship. Boundaries are not only foundational and fundamental in a relationship, but they are also essential for your own mental and physical health.

They protect your emotional and physical need for space, autonomy, independence, and rest. Boundaries make sure that your needs are met in addition to the needs of the other person. They keep us from sacrificing so much that we are left with nothing to give to the relationship, let alone ourselves.

Boundaries ensure safety and security in a relationship. They provide predictability and stability, as well as safety instead of inconsistency and feeling like you never know what to expect. By communicating what is okay and what is not, you are able to reduce confusion, assumptions, and misunderstandings.

Others can only respect the things or limits they know, see, and are clear to them. It is unfair to assume that another knows exactly what you need if you haven’t told them. This is one of the fundamental parts of communication: being clear with needs, expectations, and priorities. Clear boundaries act like a road map in the relationship to establish the routes appropriate and those that are not.

People Pleasing

Boundaries are essential for our ability to have emotional regulation and, thus, self-respect. It is important to say “no” if that is the right answer for you. People-pleasing is the antithesis to health boundaries. We are often people-pleasers because we are afraid of rejection, judgment, or abandonment. If I say “no” to something I don’t want to do, it means I face the possibility of the other person not liking me, thinking less of me, judging me, or leaving altogether.

I don’t feel like I can deal with that happening, so I say “yes” even when it is something I don’t want to do, don’t care about, am not feeling up to it, or, worse, that I disagree with. This causes me to compromise my sense of security, safety, autonomy, and even our health.

People-pleasing often comes out of our trauma, particularly childhood trauma. If you were rejected, judged, or abandoned, the hurt completely disrupted your life. Therefore, you don’t ever want to feel that pain again, so you go out of your way to make sure that doesn’t happen again. You end up running yourself into the ground, sacrificing your health, sanity, and even your identity.

You do so much for everyone else you forget what is important for you. Saying “no” is part of asking for respect, space, or expressing your needs and reinforcing that your feelings and needs matter. This helps build self-worth over time, and it prevents burnout, especially as a caregiver or in codependency.

By stopping people-pleasing and taking care of yourself, the boundaries you set strengthen your connections, instead of weakening them. It seems counterintuitive because your people-pleasing was because you wanted relationships and so that others wouldn’t leave you. Instead, it causes others to take advantage of you, create toxicity and dependency, and not only destroys you, but it also destroys the relationship.

Just like a house’s foundation is built to provide structure, separation, and defining characteristics that set a house apart from others, boundaries do this for our relationships. They allow both parties in a relationship to show up authentically, rather than out of obligation, fear, or guilt. When each person has an equal part in the relationship and maintains their individuality, the relationship becomes a willing choice rather than an obligation or a survival strategy.

Boundaries and Conflict

Boundaries help us not only manage conflict but find resolution to it. Face it, most of us fear conflict. Some thrive on it, but most avoid it. Why do you fear it so much? Because conflict involves uncomfortable emotions, unpredictability, emotional dysregulation, unknown outcomes, rejection, judgment, criticism, and can involve an ending to the relationship.

Boundaries help define our conflict, establish rules you are both comfortable with, and set limits or barriers that are not to be crossed, while allowing both parties to take time out. Conflict brings intense emotions, and you may struggle to answer logically, rationally, or with purpose when you are emotional. When emotions are allowed to enter the conflict, the chance of resolution is often lost, and there is a certainty of more hurt and/or resentment on both sides.

Boundaries for conflict should be established before the conflict happens. This ensures that the conflict will end in resolution, healthy compromise, and both parties gaining rather than losing. The structure that boundaries bring allows you to say, “I’m willing to discuss this but not if yelling, name-calling, or blaming occurs.” This keeps communication respectful, productive, safe, and guarantees resolution.

Finally, boundaries prevent you from being stuck or stagnant, protect you from toxicity or being taken advantage of, keep you safe, and allow you to maintain control and respect. They guarantee that your needs are just as important as someone else’s. Boundaries help you maintain stability, protect your physical and mental health, allow you to establish rules, and define what is unacceptable.

Healthy boundaries allow you to define situations according to your values and what are most important to you. It stops others from running over your needs, wants, or autonomy. They ensure that you can stay authentic, are worthy of respect, and protect the erosion of your identity, wants, and needs. This means that you can interrupt the repetition of unhealthy patterns and can create a relationship that is more intentional and stable.

In summary, boundaries are not walls meant to keep people out. They are doors with locks, allowing you to decide what comes in, what stays out, and who gets a key. They are the invisible fences that protect your sense of self-worth.

item.title: Dealing With Trauma: Steps Toward Faith-based Healing
item.description:
Trauma is any experience that causes deep emotional pain and can cause deep wounds that affect a person’s mind, body, and spirit. There are many causes of trauma, including abuse, loss, violence, betrayal, illness, or natural disasters.

These painful life experiences often change the way a person views themselves, others, and even God. The emotional pain may be carried silently for years, and a person may feel trapped by shame, fear, anxiety, anger, sadness, or all these emotions. Healing is possible with support, faith, and perseverance.

Trauma and the Bible

There are many stories in the Bible of people who experience grief, heartbreak, persecution, abuse, betrayal, and other forms of emotional pain. God understands trauma because He sees every person and the emotional wounds they experience.

He promises to draw close to the brokenhearted. Through faith, a person can find comfort, strength, and direction during the healing journey. Faith does not prevent or protect us from trauma; however, it provides a pathway for healing.

Trauma is more than a bad memory. It is an emotional response to a deeply distressing experience that overwhelms a person’s ability to cope. Trauma may be a single event or repeated events over a span of time.

After trauma, a person may experience difficulty sleeping, focusing, regulating their emotions, eating, interacting with others, or taking care of themselves. People may struggle with anxiety, panic, emotional numbness, distrust, shame, or feelings of worthlessness.

It is important to remember that reacting to trauma is not an indication of weakness or a lack of faith. Many people in the Bible who had a strong faith faced emotional suffering. David cried out in despair in the Psalms. Elijah experienced deep exhaustion and hopelessness. Even Jesus experienced anguish and sorrow.

God never condemns people for experiencing emotional pain. God offers comfort and healing. Psalm 34:18 states that “the Lord is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit.”

Acknowledging the Pain

One of the first steps on the pathway to healing is to acknowledge the pain instead of avoiding or hiding it. Often, people try to suppress or minimize their emotional pain from trauma because of the fear of being judged as weak, dramatic, or attention-seeking.

Others may think they should simply “move on” and count their blessings. However, people can feel blessed and have emotional pain at the same time. Ignoring the impact of trauma often causes it to grow stronger and deeper.

The Bible encourages people to be honest before God. The Psalms are filled with prayers of grief, confusion, fear, and anger. Emotional pain can only be healed when it is brought into the light and shared with others, whether it is a counselor, pastor, support group, or trusted friend. Healing happens in community rather than isolation.

Distorted Thinking

Trauma can distort thinking patterns and may cause feelings of being unloved, powerless, or worthless. These feelings and thoughts can become strongholds that affect daily life. The Bible reminds us in Romans 12:12 not to be conformed to the pattern of this world but to be transformed by the renewing of our minds.

Being abused may bring thoughts and feelings that a person is damaged and unlovable; however, God says that we are fearfully and wonderfully made in Psalm 139:14. Betrayal and loss of loved ones may create an overwhelming feeling of being all alone, but in Hebrews 13:5, God says that He will never leave us or forsake us.

One step in the pathway to healing is reading Scripture regularly, as this can help reshape distorted thoughts and bring comfort. Prayer is another step that creates a space to express fears and pain to God. The book of Lamentations is all about crying out to God when in pain.

Counseling for Trauma

Another step may be to see a counselor. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) helps identify unhealthy thinking patterns and replace them with healthier beliefs. God tells us to take every thought captive and to renew our minds, which is the formula for CBT. Some specific techniques include journaling or therapeutic letters, expressing thoughts through art, learning relaxation skills, challenging negative thoughts, and gradual exposure to feared situations.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) is an effective technique for trauma recovery. During EMDR, the therapist guides the person through traumatic memories while using bilateral stimulation, such as eye movements or tapping, to help the brain reprocess difficult memories so they are not so overwhelming.

Somatic Therapy focuses on how trauma impacts the body. Trauma often causes chronic tension, increased startle response, hypervigilance, fatigue, or other physical pain. A counselor can help a person become aware of their body and learn grounding techniques, gentle movements, deep breathing, and relaxation training. All of these can help a person’s nervous system, which may stay overstimulated even after the initial traumatic experience calms down.

Psalm 46:10 reminds us to be still and know that He is God. This isn’t only referring to physical stillness, but mental stillness.

Sometimes, groups are more effective than individual therapy, as healing often occurs when people know they are not alone and have others with whom to share encouragement, empathy, and connection, reducing shame and fear. Seeing others in the group who are further along on the pathway to healing can provide hope.

The Bible tells us to carry each other’s burdens and that “two are better than one…if either of them falls down, one can help the other up.” Also, the prayers of the faithful are effective.

The Path Forward in Dealing With Trauma

Healing does not mean forgetting the past, but that it is no longer controlling your life. A person does not need to know which path to take before starting, but simply taking one step toward healing, and often the first step is the hardest. Praying that God will show you the path and bring the people into your life who can help you heal may be the first step. Or just acknowledging that help is needed is not a sign of weakness but takes courage and strength.

The path to healing from trauma is not fast or easy, but necessary, as trauma can keep a person stuck in pain or numbness. Most people will experience some sort of trauma in their life, and the Bible tells us that we will experience trials, but that God will be present through the suffering.

With healing, a person will strengthen faith, build character, and develop a deeper relationship with God. Even though Scripture never states that the Christian life is free from trauma, it does offer hope, endurance, and purpose during difficult times.

Trauma, once healed, can become our testimony. We can find purpose from our pain. This is why it is imperative to seek healing, rather than avoiding, hiding, or trying to run from the impact of trauma. Healing is possible when we seek it, and there is a pathway for everyone.

If you are ready to find your path to healing but don’t know where to start, reach out to a counselor or pastor. As a counselor, I would be honored to walk with you on your healing journey. Please call 469-943-2962 to schedule an appointment. God bless.

item.title: Finding Help When You’re Feeling Depressed: Types of Depression Therapy
item.description:
Depression affects millions of people each year in the United States and can lead to physical and mental conditions, issues at work, and problems in relationships. Depression isolates you from others, including your spouse and children. This mental condition makes it challenging to hold conversations and focus at work.

The good news is that there are several depression therapy options available. A counselor can customize a treatment plan to address your symptoms, contributing factors to depression, and treatment goals. Knowing the types of depression therapy will prepare you for an assessment and the initial session. You want to be an advocate for your mental health. We want you to be aware of every step along your journey.

Symptoms of Depression

The symptoms of depression can vary from mild to severe. Those with mild cases may experience depressive episodes for a few weeks or during specific seasons, such as winter, when there is less sunlight.

Those with more severe symptoms may have a personal or family history or be at a higher risk due to genetics. Specific conditions can make depression symptoms more severe. A counselor will assess your symptoms to determine appropriate depression therapy.

Persistent Sadness Depression is marked by persistent sadness. This goes beyond simply feeling blue after a loss or let down after a disappointment. This pervasive sadness interferes with every aspect of your life. It may feel as if a dark cloud follows you. Although depression is temporary, sadness can feel as if it will never end.

Loss of Interest in Enjoyable Activities Losing interest in activities that once pleased you is another common depression symptom. You just “don’t feel like it” anymore. Although you love your friends and family, spending time with them feels like too much effort.

Fatigue Depression creates a loss of motivation and drive, making it more difficult to go about your daily activities. On a physiological level, changes in brain chemistry and chronic inflammation can worsen fatigue and depression symptoms. When you feel exhausted, you are more likely to miss work and skip attending family functions or events.

Feeling Hopeless or Lost Depression can cause feelings of helplessness, hopelessness, emptiness, and emotional numbness. For some people, depression leaves them feeling lost. The “why bother?” question hangs in the air. This is also a dangerous time for negative and intrusive thoughts, false beliefs, and suicidal ideation to emerge.

Mood Swings Whether due to chemical imbalances or changes in brain structure or function, mood swings and irritability are common in depression. You may feel on edge or also suffer from anxiety. Some people move through manic episodes followed by depressive episodes (bipolar disorder).

Trouble Concentrating Depression affects cognitive function and ability, making it harder to concentrate. Cortisol, a stress hormone, can damage parts of the brain, such as the hippocampus, responsible for memory, after prolonged bouts of stress. Depression and stress can go hand in hand. Managing stress can improve mood and cognitive function.

If you are struggling with depression symptoms, take heart. Feeling blue is a normal reaction to loss or disappointment, but if you experience symptoms for more than two weeks, notice that symptoms interfere with your daily activities, or have self-harm or suicidal thoughts, seek help immediately. Depression therapy combined with faith-based principles may be the answer to overcoming and healing from the mental condition.

Types of Depression Therapy

Several depression therapy treatments exist and are effective for managing symptoms and overcoming the condition. A counselor will determine the type of depression therapy used. This is dependent on your symptoms, the severity of symptoms, the type of depression, the cause of depression, your history, and what works best for you.

For example, if your depression is due to trauma, your Christian counselor may suggest a combination of talk therapy, group counseling, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) to address the trauma memory and change any negative thoughts or beliefs. Teaching new coping mechanisms takes practice, and you may have “homework” to complete between sessions.

When it comes to depression therapy, the one that will effectively work for you will be based on several factors. Your counselor will run an assessment to determine different strategies. Although many mental health care professionals turn to the most common depression therapy techniques, other types of treatment also exist.

The following are common treatments in depression therapy.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a therapy used widely to treat various mental health conditions. It is effective in treating depression, anxiety, eating disorders, addiction, OCD, and more. Thoughts, emotions, and behaviors are linked. A negative thought can influence feelings and resulting behaviors. CBT works to break the negative cycle by changing the way you think or behave to influence emotions.

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT)

Interpersonal Therapy (IPT) is a short-term therapy that addresses factors that may be causing or worsening depression. These factors can include grief, death of a loved one, good or bad life events, and relationship problems. IPT teaches you healthy coping mechanisms, conflict resolution, anger management, communication skills, and relationship skills.

Group Therapy

Support group therapy is often led by a counselor or another mental health practitioner. These groups provide a safe place to voice your worries and concerns. You receive encouragement and support from participants as well as their advice on how to manage situations. Listening to others’ stories reminds us that we are not alone.

Other Types of Depression Therapy

Not all counselors use the same depression treatments as they personalize therapies to their clients. In Christian counseling, clients learn to overcome mental health conditions while growing in their faith in God. Your counselor may use a combination of therapies or techniques to help you. You may practice a technique during a session, then use other methods in between sessions, giving feedback at the next session.

Combination of Talk Therapy and CBT

A common combination seen is psychotherapy and CBT. The counselor may spend time allowing the client to share their experiences and feelings and helping them to analyze the root cause. They will also address CBT principles to help the client identify negative thoughts and beliefs to alter emotions and behaviors.

Digital Therapeutics

Digital therapeutics are self-guided apps, either used alone or in conjunction with a mental health care practitioner. Therapies, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy, are used to help clients through an app. These therapy apps are advertised for specific conditions, like depression, postpartum, and eating disorders.

If you also take medication for depression, your prescriber may recommend an app created by the prescription drug manufacturer. Your counselor can provide you with resources and advice concerning digital apps for depression.

Psychoanalytic Therapy

Well-known for being the stereotypical “psychologist’s couch,” psychoanalytic therapy helps clients understand their own thoughts and feelings surrounding memories or current problems. Sessions are now held in the office or online, making it easier for clients to speak to their counselor from the comfort of home. This often proves to be easier for helping clients relax and open up about issues.

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR)

Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) is an effective trauma treatment. If your depression stems from trauma, EMDR might be a depression therapy to try. The client is taught bilateral eye movements in conjunction with the traumatic memory. Within a few sessions, the client should be able to recall the memory without the distressing emotions.

Depression Therapy in Your Area

Depression therapy is available in your local area, both at our Christian counseling center and in a virtual format. Clients choose the format that serves them best in this season of their lives. Many people love the convenience of virtual sessions. Contact our office today to speak to a representative, who will match you with a Christian counselor. Your counselor will work with you to discover the best depression therapy for your needs.

item.title: Have I Just Had a Traumatic Experience? Signs and Ways to Recover from Trauma
item.description:
Words are some of the most precious gifts the Lord has given us. Using our words, we can describe ourselves, our experiences, and the world around us. When we name something, it allows us to understand it better. In fact, the Bible talks directly about the power of words in Proverbs 18:21: “The tongue has the power of life and death.”

The same goes when you have a traumatic experience. Understanding what trauma is and naming your trauma appropriately can help you begin recovering from the effects of a devastating experience.

We live in a world that is broken and fallen (Genesis 3). This doesn’t mean there’s nothing good in the world. On the contrary, there is much to celebrate. However, amid the beauty, there is also pain, even in something as beautiful and creative as childbirth or a romantic relationship. Pain, hardship, and loss touch us all in one way or another as we make our way through life. Traumatic experiences are part of the fabric of the world we live in.

Understanding and Naming Trauma After a Traumatic Experience

After you’ve gone through something, you may be the sort of person who pauses, reflects, and asks, “What was that?” Perhaps it’s a painful breakup or divorce, or maybe you were involved in a bad traffic accident, and you’re still trying to put the pieces back together. Some people have been the victims of crime, and they struggle to make sense of their feelings after the fact.

After certain difficult experiences, you may be prompted to ask whether you’ve just gone through a traumatic event. You may even want to know how you’d know if something you’ve been through has traumatized you. Beyond that, you might also be asking how to find healing in Christ so that the experience doesn’t have a hold on you, and it doesn’t have the final say in who you are and how you live your life.

Trauma can be understood as the psychological and emotional response a person has to an experience that they find disturbing or deeply distressing. These kinds of experiences tend to overwhelm an individual’s ability to cope with them.

It’s a bit like when a circuit is overloaded and it trips, shutting down. To talk about trauma is mainly to talk about how our bodies and minds experience and try to make sense of what just happened.

While trauma is less about the event itself and more about how that event is processed, certain events tend to overwhelm our ability to cope with them. Though we are wired differently and don’t all have the same level of resilience or ability to cope, there are certain kinds of events that most people would find overwhelming. These include witnessing violence or experiencing physical, emotional, or sexual abuse.

Other examples of experiences that could result in trauma are natural disasters like a tsunami, earthquake, or wildfire. Being caught in a serious accident or having a sudden and serious health crisis can also be the cause of trauma. Various situations where you may have felt either powerless, unsafe, or threatened may lie at the root of trauma as well.

Trauma is not only the result of situations where you find yourself in physical danger. Trauma can be experienced by the sudden loss of a loved one, if you experience deep betrayal, or if you are abandoned by a loved one.

These and other kinds of experiences can contribute to trauma. It is important to remember that even though two people experience the exact same event, they won’t necessarily develop trauma. Trauma and being traumatized depend on how the individual experiences the moment, and that includes how it impacts one’s sense of meaning, control, and their sense of safety as well.

The Signs of Trauma to Look Out for

If you’ve gone through some things and you’re wondering if the experience has traumatized you, there are several signs of trauma that you can keep an eye out for. Trauma manifests in various ways, on the heels of the event, but also over time. There are some signs to consider as you reflect on your experience. These include:

Physical and behavioral signs of trauma Physical symptoms such as stomach pains, headaches, or unexplained muscle tension. These also include struggling to sleep or having recurring nightmares. Behaviors such as avoiding reminders of the experience or social withdrawal are also signs of trauma. Lastly, feeling on edge and struggling to concentrate also point to trauma.

Emotional and mental signs Feelings such as anxiety, panic, or a lingering sense of dread are suggestive of anxiety. Other emotions such as shock, numbness, and intense fear are also signs of trauma. Trauma and the ensuing loss of a sense of safety could result in irritability, mood swings, or anger. Additionally, you may feel disconnected or emotionally detached from your loved ones or from life.

Another possible sign of trauma is when one experiences dreams, intrusive thoughts, or even flashbacks from the experience. These can be deeply upsetting, making it feel like you’re experiencing it all over again.

Spiritual signs Trauma can manifest as a feeling of being distant from God or as though He has abandoned you. Struggling to pray or read Scripture, as well as intensely questioning and wrestling with God’s protection or goodness, may also point to trauma.

These various responses to a difficult experience may begin to hinder daily functioning. When they persist or intensify, it begins to suggest that the experience was more than simply upsetting; it has become traumatic.

Recovering from Trauma and Moving Toward Healing

Why is it that some people will experience a traumatic event, but they won’t necessarily be traumatized? People process and recover from challenging circumstances and experiences differently, and certain factors can render trauma more likely. Getting a handle on these can be a help in mitigating the impact of traumatic experiences and in building greater resilience.

Trauma is often more likely when one is exposed repeatedly or over a long time to dangerous or harmful situations and experiences. An example is when a person is repeatedly abused, or a second responder who finds their life under threat on multiple occasions. Trauma may also result when the event itself is sudden, deeply shocking, or involves being helpless. A deadly natural disaster is an example of this sort of event.

Other things that can make trauma more likely are when the individual feels like they are alone and without emotional support. We all need people around us to care for us and to be sounding boards for us when we go through crises. Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 states, “Two are better than one . . . if either of them falls down, one can help the other up.”

Being alone strips you of additional capacity to deal with difficult circumstances. Lastly, experiences that shake your core beliefs about your safety or your trust in God’s presence can also result in trauma.

Recovering from trauma is a journey. You can’t get there all at once, but it’s possible to heal and find yourself as well as your sense of safety and meaning again. Some steps that may be helpful along this journey include:

Naming the pain It’s important to acknowledge what you’ve gone through, and to name it for what it is. Be honest with the Lord and with yourself about what you’ve gone through. He knows you and loves you, through and through (Psalm 139), and He can meet you in your pain.

Pray and lament You can bring the pain, insecurity, loss of meaning, and everything else the traumatic experience has robbed you of or brought into your life and take it to the Lord in prayer. There are many Psalms of lament, like Psalm 6, 13, or 22, that can help you to give utterance to your confusion, grief, and fear even as you lean into God’s unfailing love. Take the time to reflect on what Scripture says about God’s character and faithful presence.

Gentle self-care Traumatic experiences and trauma wrench you out of what you know into new and painful territory. Instead of leaning into self-destructive behaviors to self-soothe or silence the pain, opt for gentle self-care. Rest, eat healthy and nourishing food, and get some exercise. Connect with other people. Small and consistent steps add up, and maintaining healthy rhythms can help you heal and regain a sense of safety and normalcy.

Get professional help In addition to seeking safe and wise support from loved ones who can help bear your burden and struggle, you can get professional help. A trauma-informed therapist can help you by offering practical tools as well as working with you through therapies to recover from trauma. They can guide you toward healing while integrating your faith as part of the process of recovery.

Seeking Help After a Traumatic Experience

Trauma isn’t the final word after a traumatic experience, and it isn’t a sign of weak faith. Instead, seeking help when dealing with trauma is a courageous and wise step. Healing, hope, and redemption are possible.

2 Corinthians 12:9 states, “Strength is made perfect in weakness.”

If you are feeling overwhelmed or unsafe after a traumatic experience, reach out to our office and speak to a representative today. They can schedule an appointment with a Christian counselor or therapist near you.
